text: Lesson 7's query worked, and worked fast. But it's worth stepping back and asking what Athena actually did behind the scenes, because that reveals a real cost this project is about to grow into.

The query asked about August 2026, but Athena scanned every byte of every one of the thirty-one files to answer it — because nothing in the table's structure told it which files it could skip. At a few megabytes total, that's completely invisible. It stops being invisible the moment orders-raw holds a year of daily exports instead of one month, because now even a single-day question scans twelve months of data to answer it.

Partitioning fixes this by organizing files into subfolders keyed on a column's value — here, date — using a dt equals value naming convention. That's the same pattern the full automated pipeline later adopts for its own nightly loads. Reorganizing the existing flat files into this layout is a one-time move per file, from orders-raw straight into a dt equals folder matching that file's date.

A partitioned layout only helps once the Glue Catalog actually knows the partitions exist, and that just means re-running the same crawler from Lesson 4. It discovers the new dt equals folders automatically, registers dt as a partition column — meaning a column that comes from the folder path, not from inside the CSV files — and the table gains one partition per folder.

Now a query filtering on a single date can use partition pruning — Athena checks the Catalog, sees exactly which dt equals folder could match, and skips every other folder entirely, without opening a single byte from them. At this project's scale that saves almost nothing in dollars. But the ratio holds at any scale, and once the raw zone grows to a year of daily files, that's the difference between a query that costs a few cents and finishes instantly, and one that costs real money and makes someone wait.

With the data organized for growth, next lesson turns to something just as important as the SQL itself — how to actually present this answer to the Operations Manager, especially given that units sold and revenue earned point to two different categories.
